biography: Cited as criticizing Anaxagoras for introducing mind as a cosmic cause but then making little use of it, resorting to mechanical explanation whenever possible. Main ancient source for the atomists' views (quoting Leucippus directly); also criticized them for not accounting for the atoms' original motion, a criticism Russell rejects as misplaced. Quoted at length giving a hostile, realistic critique of the Spartan constitution (its treatment of women, its inequality of property, the corruptibility and excessive power of the ephors), written after Sparta's decline. Central subject: Russell examines his biography, his critique of Plato's Ideas, his doctrines of universals, matter and form, potentiality and actuality, his theology of the unmoved mover, and his account of the soul and mind. Author of the Nicomachean Ethics; Russell reconstructs his account of happiness, virtue, the golden mean, justice, friendship, pleasure, and contemplation, and closes with a sustained critical evaluation of the whole work. Primary subject: Russell reconstructs the Politics's account of the State's natural origin, slavery, trade and usury, critique of Plato's Republic, sixfold constitutional taxonomy, analysis of revolution and tyranny, and views on State size, citizenship, and education. Primary subject: Russell reconstructs the theory of the syllogism, the doctrine of the Categories, and the treatment of essence and substance in the Posterior Analytics, before subjecting each to detailed logical and metaphysical criticism. Primary subject: Russell reconstructs the imaginative background, the teleological theory of nature, the theory of motion, the treatment of time, the argument for an unmoved mover, and the sublunary/supralunary cosmology of On the Heavens. Quoted briefly as representative of the ordinary Greek assumption that Greeks alone combine spirit and civilization, and that non-Greeks could rightly be enslaved -- the attitude Alexander's policies began to erode. A larger influence on Plotinus than is openly acknowledged, with borrowings frequently unattributed; Plotinus explicitly rejects Aristotle's view (unnamed but clearly referenced) that the soul is simply the form of the body, arguing this would make the soul's intellectual activity impossible. Grouped with Plato as holding the Greek view that substance is eternal and uncreated, with only form due to God's will; in The City of God, ranked by Augustine as Plato's inferior but far above other philosophers.
central_doctrines: The Third Man argument against Plato's theory of Ideas: Aristotle's argument, already foreshadowed in Plato's own Parmenides, that when several individuals share a predicate, this sharing cannot be explained by their all resembling a further individual of the same kind (however 'ideal'), since that would require a yet more ideal exemplar to explain the new resemblance, generating an infinite regress. Universals and substances ('this' versus 'such'): Aristotle's definition: 'By the term universal I mean that which is of such a nature as to be predicated of many subjects, by individual that which is not thus predicated.' A substance is a 'this'; a universal is a 'such,' indicating a sort of thing rather than a particular thing, and (Aristotle holds) cannot itself be a substance, since substance is 'peculiar' to one thing while a universal is common to many. Matter and Form: Aristotle's doctrine that concrete substances are compounds of matter (potentiality) and form (the principle that confers definiteness, unity, and actuality); form is said to be more real and more substantial than matter, and things become more 'actual' as they acquire more form. The Unmoved Mover and Aristotle's theology: Aristotle's argument for God as an eternal, unmoved, immaterial substance -- 'pure form and pure actuality' -- that causes motion as a final cause (the object of desire and of thought) rather than as an efficient cause; God's activity is pure self-directed thought, 'a thinking on thinking,' with no knowledge of or love for the world. The soul as form of the body, and the immortality of mind alone: In Aristotle's On the Soul, the soul is 'the actuality of a body' having life potentially within it -- related to the body as form to matter -- and is therefore, for the most part, inseparable from the body and perishes with it. Mind (nous), however, is described as 'an independent substance implanted within the soul,' timeless because its objects (mathematics, philosophy) are timeless, and 'incapable of being destroyed'; the Nicomachean Ethics adds that the rational soul's contemplative activity is the highest happiness, in which a person 'shares in the divine life' impersonally rather than as an individual. Happiness as activity of the soul in accordance with virtue: Aristotle's central ethical claim that 'the good' is happiness (eudaimonia), and that happiness consists in 'activity of soul in accordance with virtue in a complete life,' with the rational soul's contemplative activity representing its highest and most complete form. The doctrine of the golden mean: The doctrine that moral virtue is a disposition to feel and act in a way that is intermediate between two vicious extremes, one of excess and one of deficiency, relative to the particular person and situation -- e.g. courage between cowardice and rashness, liberality between prodigality and meanness, proper pride between vanity and humility. The magnanimous (great-souled) man: Aristotle's description of megalopsychia ('great-souledness,' rendered 'magnanimous' by Russell rather than 'proud'): the crowning virtue that presupposes and enhances all the others, concerned chiefly with great honours and dishonours, and possible in practice only for someone of exceptional social position, wealth, and virtue. Justice as proportion rather than equality: Aristotle's view that justice involves 'not equality, but right proportion, which is only sometimes equality,' so that, for example, the superior in an unequal relationship (husband, parent, master) may rightly receive more honour or love than they give, and political power may rightly be distributed unevenly according to virtue. Contemplation as the highest happiness: Aristotle's culminating doctrine that perfect happiness lies in the best activity, contemplation, since it alone offers leisure and is 'preferable to war or politics or any other practical career'; the philosopher, being most akin to God in exercising reason, is 'the dearest to the gods' and therefore the happiest of men. The State as natural and prior to the individual: Aristotle's organic conception of political community, in which the State, though the last stage in a natural sequence of family and village, is metaphysically prior to its parts because 'what each thing is when fully developed we call its nature,' and a part (like a severed hand) can be defined only by the function it performs within the functioning whole. Natural slavery: Aristotle's doctrine that certain individuals are naturally inferior in reason and thus fit only for subjection ('the man who is by nature not his own but another man's is by nature a slave'), that slavery of such persons is expedient and just, and that war waged against peoples who by nature ought to be ruled but refuse to submit is likewise just. Critique of trade and usury: Aristotle's economic doctrine (Politics I) that wealth acquired through household management of land is natural and has a proper limit, while wealth acquired through retail trade is unnatural and unlimited, with usury -- 'a gain out of money itself, and not from the natural object of it' -- condemned as the most unnatural mode of acquisition of all. Sixfold classification of constitutions: Aristotle's taxonomy distinguishing governments by whether rulers pursue the common good (monarchy, aristocracy, polity) or their own narrow interest (tyranny, oligarchy, democracy respectively), further cross-cut by an economic criterion distinguishing oligarchy (rule by the rich, disregarding the poor) from democracy (rule by the poor/many, disregarding the rich). The anatomy of tyranny: Aristotle's description, in an 'ironically Machiavellian tone,' of the practical techniques by which a tyrant retains power: suppressing potential rivals, prohibiting associations and education likely to foster hostile solidarity, maintaining surveillance through informers, sowing internal discord, impoverishing subjects, and engaging in constant public works or war to keep the population occupied and dependent on a leader. The syllogism: Aristotle's central logical form, an argument of exactly three parts (major premiss, minor premiss, conclusion) sorted by the scholastics into named figures and moods (e.g. 'Barbara,' 'Celarent,' 'Darii,' 'Ferio' in the first figure), with a second and third figure reducible to the first, and a fourth figure later added by medieval logicians. Formal defects: existential import and the particular/universal confusion: Russell's critique that Aristotelian universal statements ('all S is P') are ambiguous between a purely hypothetical reading (which does not imply that any S exists) and a reading that presupposes S is non-empty, and that several of Aristotle's syllogisms are valid only under the latter, existentially-loaded reading -- a distinction Aristotle's system never makes explicit. Over-estimation of deduction relative to induction: Russell's claim that, apart from logic and pure mathematics, virtually all substantive inference outside law and theology (which derive their first principles from an unquestionable text) is inductive rather than deductive, contrary to the excessive prominence Greek philosophy, including Aristotle's own theory of knowledge, gives to deduction from general premises. Essence: Aristotle's notion, central to the Posterior Analytics's account of definition and first premisses, that a thing's essential properties are those it cannot change without losing its identity, as opposed to accidental properties (like being happy or sad) that it can change while remaining the same thing; Russell calls this 'a hopelessly muddle-headed notion' whose real content is purely linguistic. Substance: The Aristotelian notion (Categories) of substance in its primary sense as an individual thing that is neither predicable of, nor present in, any other subject, later extended (in a 'secondary' sense Russell finds indefensible) to species and genera; Russell argues on independent grounds that substance, taken seriously as something distinct from all its properties, is 'a metaphysical mistake, due to transference to the world-structure of the structure of sentences composed of a subject and a predicate.' The imaginative background of physics: Will as the source of motion: Russell's own interpretive thesis (borrowing Santayana's phrase 'animal faith') that beneath Aristotle's explicit physical doctrines lies an unstated, pre-theoretical picture in which motion is modeled on animal self-movement and the willed regularity of divinized heavenly bodies, rather than on the strictly mechanical picture of later physics. Nature (phusis) as teleological: Aristotle's technical concept of phusis as a thing's end (that for the sake of which it exists), applied to whatever possesses an internal principle of motion or rest (broadly construed to include qualitative and quantitative change, not just locomotion), with a thing being 'more what it is' the closer it approaches its fulfilled, actualized form. Motion as the actualization of potential: Aristotle's account of motion (kinesis) as the process by which a potentially existing state becomes actual, a definition that presupposes an absolute, non-relative distinction between a moving thing and a thing at rest, incompatible with the principle (basic to later physics) that locomotion can only be described relative to some reference body. Sublunary versus supralunary cosmology (the fifth element): The cosmology of On the Heavens, dividing the universe into a corruptible sublunary region composed of the four terrestrial elements (whose natural motions are rectilinear: fire and air upward, earth and water downward, in proportion to relative 'lightness' and 'heaviness') and an eternal, incorruptible supralunary region composed of a fifth element, whose only natural motion is perfect circular rotation, carrying the stars and planets on attached spheres.

russell_view: Russell opens by insisting Aristotle be judged fairly on both sides: his merits relative to his predecessors were enormous, but his two-thousand-year unquestioned authority did enormous damage to later science and philosophy, for which his successors, not Aristotle himself, are chiefly to blame. He characterizes Aristotle's temperament as unemotional, professorial, and pedestrian compared to Plato's 'Bacchic enthusiasm,' and is skeptical that Aristotle had much real influence on Alexander despite their famous tutorial relationship. Turning to metaphysics, Russell credits Aristotle's criticism of Plato's Ideas (especially the Third Man argument) as genuinely decisive, but judges Aristotle's own replacement doctrine of universals to be unclear, and -- following Zeller -- argues that Aristotle's doctrine of form remains covertly Platonic, exposing Aristotle to versions of his own objections against Plato. He presents the theology of the unmoved mover in detail, including the puzzling multiplication of movers, and treats Aristotle's optimistic, teleological picture of a universe evolving toward God as intellectually interesting but resting on the dubious, unanalysed notion of potentiality. On the soul, Russell reconstructs Aristotle's view carefully, concluding that the most natural interpretation makes the immortality of 'mind' impersonal rather than a survival of the individual self.
why_this_matters: Russell judges Aristotle's Third Man argument to be a genuinely decisive objection to Plato's theory of Ideas, even though it left the problem of universals unsolved. Aristotle's own doctrine of universals ('substance' as 'this,' 'universal' as 'such') rests, on Russell's analysis, on a merely linguistic (subject/predicate) distinction rather than a genuine metaphysical one.
